title: Lo vs Le: Direct and Indirect Object Pronouns in Spanish

body_html:
Lo vs le is one of the most confusing points of Spanish grammar, even for native speakers, who don’t always agree. The basic rule is simple: lo and la replace the direct object (what or whom), while le replaces the indirect object (to or for whom). Lo veo (I see him/it) vs Le doy el libro (I give him the book). Then come regional habits like leísmo in Spain, and a few verbs that behave differently. Here’s a clear path through it.

Quick answer
  • Lo / la / los / las = direct object: La llamo. I call her.
  • Le / les = indirect object: Le escribo. I write to her.
  • Indirect objects don’t change for gender: le = to him, to her, to you (usted).
  • In Spain, le is also accepted for a male person as direct object: Le vi (leísmo).
{{toc}}

Lo vs le: the core rule

Direct objectIndirect object
AnswersWhat? Whom?To whom? For whom?
Singularlo (masc.), la (fem.)le
Plurallos, lasles
ExampleCompré el pan. Lo compré.Escribí a Ana. Le escribí.

The RAE’s Diccionario panhispánico de dudas explains the standard system and the regional variations known as leísmo, laísmo and loísmo.

The passive test

A quick test for the direct object: can you make the sentence passive? Juan ve a María → María es vista por Juan. Yes, so María is the direct object: Juan la ve. With an indirect object it doesn’t work: Juan escribe a María → *María es escrita. So: Juan le escribe.

Sentences with both

When both appear, the indirect object pronoun goes first, and le becomes se before lo, la, los, las:

  • Le doy el regalo a mi madre. → Se lo doy.
  • Les explico la lección a los alumnos. → Se la explico.

More on pronoun order in {{link:spanish-word-order|Spanish word order}}.

{{image:2}}

Leísmo: le for a male person

In much of Spain, people say Le vi ayer (I saw him yesterday) instead of Lo vi. The RAE accepts this leísmo for male persons in the singular, because it is so widespread. Using le for things (El libro le compré) or for women (A María le vi) is not accepted. In Latin America, lo is the norm: Lo vi ayer. If you want one safe system, use lo/la for direct objects everywhere.

Laísmo and loísmo

In parts of central Spain you may hear La dije que viniera (using la for an indirect object). This laísmo is considered incorrect; standard is Le dije. Using lo as indirect object (loísmo) is rarer and also incorrect.

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Usted and le

With usted, the direct object is lo or la depending on the person’s gender: Lo espero, señor / La espero, señora. Many speakers prefer le as a mark of respect for both, especially in Spain: Le espero en la oficina. See {{link:tu-vs-usted|tú vs usted}}.

Verbs that surprise learners

  • Gustar, encantar, doler, parecer take le: Le gusta el cine. See {{link:how-to-use-gustar|how to use gustar}}.
  • Ayudar takes a direct object: La ayudo, though le ayudo is common.
  • Llamar (to call) takes a direct object: La llamé.
  • Pegar (to hit) and robar (to steal from) take le: Le robaron la cartera.

Why this pair is tricky for learners

English pronouns don’t show the difference: “I gave him the book” and “I saw him” both use “him”. Spanish separates them, and the line doesn’t always match English prepositions. “I called her” has no “to”, but “I phoned her” might feel like “to her” in English; in Spanish both are direct: la llamé. The safest strategy is to learn verbs with their pattern, like ayudar a alguien (direct) and escribirle a alguien (indirect), and check with the passive test when in doubt.

Tip: when unsure, replace the object with a noun and look for the preposition a meaning “to”. If it fits, it is indirect.

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
La dije la verdad.Le dije la verdad.Indirect object: le
Le lo di.Se lo di.le + lo → se lo
El carro le vendí.El carro lo vendí.Things: lo
Les vi a ellas.Las vi.Female direct object: las
La gusta.Le gusta.Gustar takes le
{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. I bought the flowers. I bought them. (Las compré.)
  2. I sent an email to my boss. I sent him an email. (Le mandé un correo.)
  3. I sent it to him. (Se lo mandé.)
  4. I called my grandmother. I called her. (La llamé.)
  5. They stole his phone. (Le robaron el celular.)

More pairs in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

What or whom: lo, la, los, las. To or for whom: le, les. Before another pronoun, le becomes se. Accept leísmo when you hear it in Spain, avoid laísmo, and you’ll handle object pronouns like an educated native speaker.

faq.q: What is the difference between lo and le?
faq.a: Lo (and la, los, las) replaces the direct object, what or whom. Le (and les) replaces the indirect object, to or for whom.
In Spain, using le for a male person as direct object (leísmo) is accepted by the RAE. In Latin America and in standard usage, lo vi is the norm.

faq.q: Why is it se lo and not le lo?
faq.a: Because le and les change to se before lo, la, los and las: Se lo di.
